On design cycles, Goodwin believes you can compress the gap between observation and volume realization, but not to shipping a new chip every few weeks, because fabs have three to five month cycle times and chips need a three to five year amortization window. His memorable line: "The equivalent of the frontier model for the chip space is if you can just find a way to structurally carve out a three to six months advantage, you will be winning all of those deployments." He also offered a heuristic for AI timelines: always question your logical assumption, then divide it by four.
https://www.youtube.com/@NoPriorsPodcast

## 🎙 PODCASTS
**Takeaway**: A chip startup is betting that the key to faster AI inference is not just raw compute, but a fundamental rethinking of memory bandwidth to handle the long contexts and massive models that power the next generation of agents.

On the **No Priors** podcast, host **Sarith** spoke with **Walter Goodwin**, founder and CEO of **Fractile**, a full-stack AI chip company building very fast inference chips for the world's largest models. Goodwin explained that while there is an "extraordinary zoo" of AI chips, many are "relatively identikit," relying on the same HBM memory and Tensor Cores. Fractile's bet is on speed, but they realized early on that an SRAM-based approach, while offering high bandwidth, wouldn't scale to the growing context lengths of modern models. This led them to a new architecture focused on achieving extremely high bandwidth to higher-capacity DRAM memories.

Goodwin argued that the real value of speed is not a "snappier chatbot" but in making long-running agents radically faster. He described a "tantalizing mismatch" today where fast inference chips have high bandwidth but low capacity, and are not running long context attention, forcing a flip back to a GPU. Fractile aims to solve this by uniting the scalability of DRAM with the speed advantages of SRAM-based chips. He believes that by compressing the chip design cycle, a company can have more shots on goal and maintain a rolling frontier of bets.

When asked about the timeline for AI to design a full chip from intent to a GDSII file, Goodwin suggested a heuristic of dividing conventional estimates by four. He noted that while final sign-off will remain with established players like **Cadence** and **Synopsys**, there is a huge opportunity for "fuzzy placement algorithms" and surrogate models to accelerate the iterative parts of chip design, much like how AI is now guiding AI model development but remains bottlenecked by compute time for experiments.

A memorable quote from Goodwin: "It's equivalent of the frontier model for the chip space is if you can just find a way to structurally carve out a three to six months advantage, you will be winning all of those deployments."

On No Priors, Walter Goodwin, founder and CEO of full-stack AI chip company **Fractile**, explained why he started the company in summer 2022 around a bet on speed for the world's largest models. He noted the physical constraints remain real: three to five month fab cycle times, three to five year amortization windows, and data center power limits, so the value is in shortening the latency between observation and volume ramp, not shipping a fundamentally new chip every few weeks.

On No Priors, host Sarith spoke with Walter Goodwin, founder and CEO of full stack AI chip company **Fractile**, about what it means to be full stack, the technical bets they're making, why he's so focused on memory bandwidth, and his predictions for frontier model architectures. **Garry Tan** of **Y Combinator** described **Capy** as a 24/7 standup for your agents, highlighting unexpected cross-session coordination where a collaborator's fix wave steered around his own work across multiple threads, all model agnostic. ## 📰 OFFICIAL BLOGS

**Claude for Small Business** now includes 43 workflows and 27 new integrations with tools small businesses already use, including **Shopify**, **Salesforce**, **TikTok**, **Atlassian**, **Zoom**, **Xero**, **Gusto**, **Square**, **Stripe**, and **Zapier**. ## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: Fractile is betting that the real bottleneck for frontier AI is not compute but memory bandwidth, and that a three to six month structural advantage in chip design wins every deployment.

On **No Priors**, **Walter Goodwin**, Founder and CEO of **Fractile**, explained why his company builds very fast inference chips for the world's largest models. He described the current chip landscape as an "extraordinary zoo" of relatively identikit chips, where hyperscalers like **Google** with **TPU**, **Meta** with **MTIA**, **Microsoft** with **Maya**, and **OpenAI** with **Jalapeno** all rely on a small number of ASIC houses, with **Broadcom** as the largest. Fractile's bet is different: after starting with an SRAM-based approach like **Groq** or **Cerebras**, they moved toward working closely with memory vendors to get extremely high bandwidth access to higher capacity **DRAM** memories. Goodwin argued that the snappier chatbot is the "faster horses" of fast inference, and the real prize is making long-running agents radically faster. He noted a tantalizing mismatch: fast inference chips have super high bandwidth but incredibly low capacity, so they cannot run long context attention and still flip back to a GPU. Fractile aims to unite the scalability of DRAM with the speed advantages of SRAM-based chips, with a platform ramping in the second half of next year. On the pace of chip design, he said he always questions logical assumptions and divides timelines by four, suggesting that intent-to-GDSII prototyping could arrive in a few years rather than ten. He also drew a parallel to RSI work: extreme intelligence can guide experiments, but then you are experiment bottlenecked, and the same applies to chip design where place and route tools still run for days.

**No Priors** hosted Walter Goodwin, Founder and CEO of **Fractile**, to discuss building full-stack AI chips for frontier labs. The key takeaway is that winning the AI chip race requires a full-stack approach to carve out a structural 3-6 month advantage over competitors.

Walter explained that **Fractile** is building very fast inference chips for the world's largest models. He noted that the current chip landscape is filled with "relatively identikit chips" from hyperscalers and ASIC houses like **Broadcom**, which all rely on similar technologies like **HBM** and **Tensor Cores**. **Fractile**'s bet is on a full-stack approach, owning everything from front-end design to physical design and advanced packaging, which allows for a more agile closed loop.

A key technical bet for **Fractile** was moving away from an **SRAM**-based chip design, which they worked on for the first two years. They became concerned about its scalability, particularly with growing context lengths. Their new focus is on working with memory vendors to achieve extremely high bandwidth access to higher-capacity **DRAM** memories. He also discussed the challenge of chip design cycles, noting that while AI can accelerate front-end design, physical constraints like fab cycle times (3-5 months) and the need for a 3-5 year amortization window remain. He believes the goal is not to ship new chips every few weeks, but to shorten the latency between an architectural observation and its realization in volume, allowing for more shots on goal.

## 🎙 PODCASTS
**Takeaway**: A full-stack chip startup is betting that raw inference speed, not just snappier chatbots, is the real capability unlock for long-running agents.

On No Priors, host Sarith spoke with Walter Goodwin, Founder and CEO of Fractile, a full-stack AI chip company building very fast inference chips for the world's largest models. Goodwin started the company in summer 2022 after seeing foundation models generalize across everything and wise voices arguing for pouring more compute into models at test time, the AlphaGo lesson brought to language modeling. Their mission: run huge models much faster than today's chips while scaling to models beyond the frontier and extraordinarily long contexts.

Goodwin described an "extraordinary zoo" of accelerators where many are relatively identikit, sharing HBM, Tensor Cores, and advanced packaging with TSMC, with a small number of ASIC houses like Broadcom delivering designs. Fractile instead goes all the way up and down the silicon stack, with front end designers, its own physical design team, back end implementation, and advanced packaging work, all at about 150 people. The bet on speed informed the architecture: after roughly two years on an SRAM-based chip like Grok or Cerebras, they grew worried about scalability as context length ballooned, and pivoted to working with memory vendors to get extremely high bandwidth access to higher capacity DRAM. The platform ramps in the second half of next year, uniting DRAM scalability with SRAM-like speed.

On where speed matters, Goodwin invoked Henry Ford: the snappier chatbot is the faster horse, while the real elevator on capability is making very long running agents radically faster. He flagged a tantalizing mismatch where fast inference chips have high bandwidth but low capacity, so long context attention still flips back to a GPU. He also argued the chip design cycle can compress, but not to shipping a new chip every few weeks, because fab cycle times run three to five months and chips need a three to five year amortization window. Asked about a top semi CEO's prediction of ten years to go from chief architect intent to a usable GDS two file, Goodwin said to divide by four and subtract a bit. His memorable line: "The equivalent of the frontier model for the chip space is if you can just find a way to structurally carve out a three to six months advantage, you will be winning all of those deployments."

He sees a dearth of efforts that go all the way up and down the silicon stack to build fundamentally new capabilities.

For the first two years, Fractile worked on an SRAM-based chip, drawn by the extremely high bandwidth between compute and weights or KV cache, which can drive thousands of tokens per second. But by late 2023 and 2024, growing context length made scalability a concern, pushing the company toward working closely with memory vendors to get extremely high bandwidth access to higher capacity DRAM. The platform ramping in the second half of next year aims to unite the scalability of DRAM with the speed advantages of SRAM-based chips. Goodwin calls the snappier chatbot "the faster horses of fast inference," and points to a tantalizing mismatch: fast inference chips have super high bandwidth but incredibly low capacity, so long context attention still flips back to a GPU.

On architecture churn, he notes models arrive about every two weeks, but sanity comes from finding what is common: LLMs always want orders of magnitude more memory bandwidth, and remain autoregressive and low batch. He is skeptical of shipping a fundamentally new chip every few weeks, citing fab cycle times of three to five months even in a hot lot scenario and the need for a three to five year amortization window. Asked about a top semi CEO's prediction of ten years until intent from a chief architect becomes a fully usable GDS2 file, Goodwin applies his heuristic: divide by four and subtract a bit. He expects end-to-end prototyping within a few years, but notes place and route still runs conventional algorithms for days, and final sign-off with Cadence and Synopsys will not change for quite some time.
https://www.youtube.com/@NoPriorsPodcast

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The chip race's real prize is not a faster chatbot but radically faster long-running agents, and whoever compresses the gap between an architectural insight and volume deployment wins the frontier.

On No Priors, Walter Goodwin, founder and CEO of full stack AI chip company **Fractile**, explains why he started in summer 2022 around two observations: foundation models generalizing across everything, and the need to pour more compute into models at test time, the way AlphaGo became superhuman when rolled out at scale. Fractile builds very fast inference chips for the world's largest models, aiming to run them far faster than today's chips while scaling to models beyond the frontier and to extraordinarily long contexts.

Goodwin describes an "extraordinary zoo" of accelerators where many are relatively identikit: HBM memory, Tensor Cores for matrix multiplication, advanced packaging at TSMC, with hyperscaler efforts like Google's TPU, Meta's MTIA, Microsoft's Maya, and OpenAI's Jalapeno largely delivered through a small number of ASIC houses, Broadcom being the largest. He argues there is a dearth of teams going all the way up and down the silicon stack, from architecture and front end design down to physical design and foundry interactions. Fractile is about 150 people, skinny in every sector but owning front end design, physical design, back end implementation, and advanced packaging in house, which lets it run a much more agile closed loop.

The technical journey is the most interesting part. For the first two years Fractile worked on an SRAM based chip, like Grok or Cerebras, exploiting SRAM's extreme bandwidth because it lives on the same silicon as the logic, driving thousands of tokens per second. Toward the end of 2023 and into 2024 they grew worried about scalability, not just model parameters but growing context length. That pushed them toward working closely with memory vendors and logic foundry partners on skunkworks projects to get much higher bandwidth to higher capacity DRAM, a platform ramping in the second half of next year that unites DRAM's scalability with SRAM-like speed. Goodwin calls the snappier chatbot the faster horses of fast inference; the real elevator on capability is making very long running agents radically faster. He notes the tantalizing mismatch today: fast inference chips have super high bandwidth but incredibly low capacity, so long context attention still flips back to a GPU.

On timelines, he questions the assumption that intent-to-GDS2 is ten years away, offering a heuristic of dividing such estimates by four. He sees prototyping end to end within a few years, but notes genuine bottlenecks: place and route tools running for days on NP hard problems, three to five month fab cycle times even on hot lots, and the need for a three to five year amortization window. His framing of the payoff is the sharpest moment of the episode: "It is the equivalent of the frontier model for the chip space: if you can just find a way to structurally carve out a three to six month advantage, you will be winning all of those deployments." The goal is a rolling frontier of bets, ready to trigger the ramp, with more shots on goal rather than a new chip every few weeks.

He expects end-to-end prototyping within a few years, with conventional place and route tools and DRC/LVS signoff remaining valuable bottlenecks for a long time. His closing image is the one that lingers: crack open an NVIDIA system and you find six to nine custom chips working together, so Fractile is trying to build the machine that gives it a rolling frontier of bets and a perennial three to six month wedge.

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: A full-stack chip startup argues that the real prize in fast inference is not a snappier chatbot but radically faster long-running agents, and that winning means structurally carving out a three to six month advantage.

On No Priors, host Sarith spoke with Walter Goodwin, founder and CEO of full-stack AI chip company **Fractile**. Goodwin explained that Fractile builds very fast inference chips for the world's largest models, a bet on speed held since the company started in summer 2022. He described a landscape full of "relatively identikit chips," where hyperscaler efforts like Google's **TPU**, Meta's **MTIA**, Microsoft's **Maya**, and OpenAI's **Jalapeno** are largely delivered in partnership with a small number of ASIC houses, Broadcom being the largest. All of them lean on the same **HBM**, Tensor Cores, and TSMC advanced packaging, leaving a dearth of teams going all the way up and down the silicon stack. Fractile, about 150 people, keeps front end design, physical design, back end implementation, and advanced packaging in house for an agile closed loop.

The technical journey is the heart of it. For the first two years, Fractile worked on an **SRAM**-based chip, like Grok or Cerebras, betting on extremely high bandwidth between compute and weights or KV cache. But scalability worries, especially growing context length, pushed them toward working with memory vendors to get extremely high bandwidth access to higher capacity **DRAM**. The platform ramping in the second half of next year aims to unite the scalability of DRAM with the speed advantages of an SRAM chip. Goodwin framed the payoff sharply: "The snappier chatbot is kind of the faster horses of kind of fast inference." The real elevator on capability is taking multi-trillion parameter models and running them at many thousands of tokens per second for very long running agents.

He also offered a memorable line on the competitive stakes: "It is the equivalent of the frontier model for the chip space: if you can just find a way to structurally carve out a three to six months advantage, you will be winning all of those deployments." On timelines, he pushed back on a top semi CEO's estimate of ten years to go from chief architect intent to a fully usable GDS2 file, saying he would divide it by four and subtract a bit. He noted that chip design still contains loops with conventional solutions to NP hard problems, like place and route running for days, and that as intelligence accelerates, those trials become the bottleneck, making approximate or surrogate approaches increasingly valuable.

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: Fractile is betting that the next chip war is won on memory bandwidth, not raw compute, and that a three to six month structural speed advantage is enough to win every frontier deployment.

On **No Priors**, host Sarith spoke with **Walter Goodwin**, Founder and CEO of **Fractile**, a full stack AI chip company building very fast inference chips for the world's largest models. Goodwin started the company in summer 2022, seeing both the arrival of foundation models and the need to pour more compute into models at test time, the way AlphaGo became superhuman when rolled out at scale. He argues the chip landscape is full of relatively identikit designs: HBM memory, Tensor Cores, advanced packaging at TSMC, with most hyperscaler efforts delivered in partnership with a small number of ASIC houses, Broadcom being the largest. Fractile instead owns the whole stack, roughly 150 people spanning workload understanding, front end design, physical design, back end implementation, and advanced packaging, which lets it run a much more agile closed loop. The company spent its first two years on an SRAM-based chip, like Grok or Cerebras, before worrying about scalability as context lengths grew. Goodwin is blunt that a snappier chatbot is the faster horses of fast inference; the real prize is making long-running agents radically faster. He notes the tantalizing mismatch today: fast inference chips have super high bandwidth but incredibly low capacity, so they cannot run long context attention and still flip back to a GPU. On timelines, he applies a heuristic of dividing conventional estimates by four, suggesting architect intent to a usable GDS two file could come in a few years rather than ten, though final signoff with Cadence and Synopsys will not change soon. He also draws a parallel to RSI work: extreme intelligence can guide experiments, but you still end up experiment and compute-time bottlenecked.

Thariq highlighted that "You should know" is a great way to stay on top of what's possible with **Claude**, calling it "a great example of the kind of things mods enable."

Guillermo Rauch praised a writeup on **Jev** and Python, and celebrated the team shipping fast.

Aditya Agarwal celebrated his second portfolio company IPO this week with **Moneyview**, reflecting on the founders' journey as "long, hard and tough as nails."

**Claude for Small Business** now includes 43 workflows and 27 new integrations with tools including **Shopify**, **Salesforce**, **TikTok**, **Atlassian**, **Zoom**, **Xero**, **Gusto**, **Square**, **Stripe**, and **Zapier**. The product has been installed more than 900,000 times since launching in May. New workflows extend Claude from back office operations to growing the business, with a fall schedule of free workshops in 10 US cities and over 750 workshops from 150+ Approved Claude SMB Trainers.

Pedro Rubio, Founder and CEO of Blackfyre GovCon, shared: "What used to take me 120 hours now takes five minutes." Cara Roellgen, Director of Strategy and Innovation at KBSO Consulting, called Claude "an equalizer for small businesses." Garrett French, Owner of Driller Design Co., described a daily briefing workflow: "At 6:00 am every morning, it goes and looks through our CRM, gets all of the to-do list items, prioritizes them, and sends out an email saying, here's what needs to be done today."

https://claude.com/blog/claude-for-small-business-launches-new-workflows-integrations-and-training-programs

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: Fractile is betting that the future of AI inference belongs to chips that combine the speed of SRAM-based designs with the capacity of DRAM, targeting long-running agents rather than just snappier chatbots.

Walter Goodwin, Founder and CEO of Fractile, joined No Priors to discuss building full-stack AI inference chips. He explained that Fractile started in summer 2022 with a bet on speed, recognizing that foundation models would need more compute at test time. The company initially worked on SRAM-based chips like Grok and Cerebras, achieving thousands of tokens per second, but grew concerned about scalability as context lengths expanded.

"We started to worry about the scalability of this approach," Goodwin said. "There are two things that grow with AI today. One is obviously the parameters of the model. But the other was this growing context length."

This led Fractile to pivot toward working with memory vendors to achieve "extremely high bandwidth access to higher capacity memories." Goodwin described the current landscape as having "a tantalizing mismatch" where fast inference chips have "super high bandwidth memory but incredibly low capacity" and can't run long context attention without flipping back to a GPU.

The company's platform, ramping in the second half of next year, aims to unite "the scalability of these higher capacity, lower cost DRAM memories that you have on a GPU, on a TPU with all of the speed advantages that you get from a Grok chip or a Cerebras chip."

Goodwin sees the real value of speed in "taking these very long running agents and making them radically faster," not just creating snappier chatbots. He compared the latter to Henry Ford's famous observation about faster horses.

On the chip design cycle, Goodwin believes AI can compress timelines significantly. "A heuristic that has been successful over the past couple of years is to just always question your logical assumption and then divide it by four on time scale." He noted that while physical constraints like fab cycle times of three to five months remain, the ability to iterate faster means "more shots on goal."

The competitive landscape includes NVIDIA systems with "anywhere between six and nine custom chips all built by NVIDIA," creating a gap Fractile hopes to close. Goodwin's goal is to build "a rolling frontier of bets" that could give a three to six month advantage: "The equivalent of the frontier model for the chip space is if you can just find a way to structurally carve out a three to six months advantage, you will be winning all of those deployments."

https://www.youtube.com/@NoPriorsPodcast

**Takeaway**: Fractile is betting that the winning chip will not be the fastest chatbot accelerator but the one that can run multi-trillion parameter models at thousands of tokens per second with economical memory.

On No Priors, Walter Goodwin, Founder and CEO of Fractile, explains why he started a full stack AI chip company in summer 2022 around a single bet: speed. He argues the frontier model equivalent for the chip space is structurally carving out a three to six month advantage, which wins all the deployments. He describes the current landscape as an extraordinary zoo of relatively identikit chips, all leaning on HBM, Tensor Cores, and TSMC advanced packaging, with front end design handed off to ASIC houses like Broadcom. Fractile instead keeps the whole story in house, about 150 people spanning workload understanding, front end design, physical design, back end implementation, and advanced packaging, to run a more agile closed loop.

The technical journey is the most interesting part. For the first two years Fractile worked on an SRAM based chip, chasing extremely high bandwidth between compute and weights or KV cache. But growing context length made scalability a worry, pushing them toward working with memory vendors to get extremely high bandwidth access to higher capacity DRAM. Goodwin calls the snappier chatbot the faster horses of fast inference; the real elevator on capability is making long-running agents radically faster. He points to a tantalizing mismatch: today's fast inference chips have super high bandwidth but incredibly low capacity, so long context attention still flips back to a GPU. The economics, he says, collapse down to cost per gigabyte of memory.

On timelines, Goodwin questions the conventional wisdom that big architectural changes move slowly. His heuristic is to take a logical assumption and divide it by four on time scale, so a ten year prediction for architect intent to a usable GDS two file becomes a few years. He notes chip design still contains NP hard loops like place and route running for days, and that as intelligence accelerates, those trials become the bottleneck, much like RSI work becoming experiment and compute time bottlenecked. He does not believe we will ship a fundamentally new chip every few weeks, because fabs have three to five month cycle times and chips need a three to five year amortization window. But compressing the gap between an observation and realizing that bet in volume is where the enormous value sits.

On timelines, Goodwin questions assumptions and divides by four. Asked how soon a chief architect's intent could become a fully usable GDS two file, he says a ten year estimate is sensible but he would divide it by four and subtract a bit, expecting end-to-end prototyping in the next few years. He compares it to the RSI question: extreme intelligence can guide experiments, but then you are experiment and compute-time bottlenecked. Final sign off will not change for quite some time, since Cadence and Synopsys have spent decades with TSMC building DRC and LVS clean checks. His most memorable line: "It is the equivalent of the frontier model for the chip space: if you can just find a way to structurally carve out a three to six months advantage, you will be winning all of those deployments."
